summary: Sets out rules that let independent multicast routing domains work together efficiently, even when they use different multicast routing protocols. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Different towns may run buses differently. These rules help their buses hand riders over so one trip works across towns.

questions: how do multicast routing protocols interoperate
how does a border router connect multicast domains
what is a multicast border router
subtitle: Rules for mixing multicast routing protocols within a single border router.

tldr.problem: Networks using different multicast routing protocols in different areas (DVMRP, MOSPF, PIM, CBT, etc.) need these domains to work together, but mixing protocols risks routing loops and dropped packets.
tldr.mechanism: Border routers can run multiple routing protocol components simultaneously by following a set of invariant rules about which component owns incoming interfaces, when to alert other components to forwarding changes, and how to coordinate joins and prunes across protocol boundaries.
tldr.outcome: This reduces the interoperability problem from O(N²) potential interactions between N protocols down to just N instantiations of the same rules, allowing any protocol to work with any other without custom bridges.

facts.label: RFCs covered
facts.value: DVMRP, MOSPF, PIM-DM, PIM-SM, CBT, IGMP

facts.label: Domain topologies
facts.value: Tree (with backbone and stubs) or arbitrary (with inter-domain protocol)

facts.label: Interoperability problem reduction
facts.value: From O(N²) protocol pairs to N instantiations of rules

today: RFC 2715 remains informational guidance for multicast border router implementations. While the original multicast protocols have seen varied deployment, the principles for interoperating independent protocol domains remain sound and are referenced by modern multicast systems.

sections.title: The Multicast Domain Problem
sections.content:
A multicast routing domain is a network region running a single multicast routing protocol. When sources and receivers exist in different domains, multicast border routers (MBRs) must connect them. Without coordination rules, packets can disappear (black holes) or loop infinitely when the router runs multiple protocols side by side.

RFC 2715 solves this by defining rules that work for any protocol. Instead of writing separate bridges between DVMRP-to-PIM, DVMRP-to-MOSPF, PIM-to-CBT and so on (which scales as O(N²)), each protocol implements the same set of rules once.
sections.eli5: Many towns with different bus systems meet at a border. Instead of teaching each system about every other, teach them all the same border rules.

sections.title: How MBRs Share a Forwarding Cache
sections.content:
An MBR has multiple routing protocol components (one per domain), each owning one or more network interfaces. All components share a single forwarding cache of (S,G) entries (source and group), but each component only controls its own interfaces. The key architectural insight is that the component owning the incoming interface (iif) decides where packets for that flow come from, while any component can list its interfaces in the outgoing list.

Rules 1 through 6 define what happens when this shared cache changes: one component must own each incoming interface, components must be alerted when new flows arrive, and components must coordinate when a flow's outgoing interfaces change so they send upstream joins or prunes.
sections.eli5: Multiple bus systems work at the same station. They share a list of which buses are carrying which passengers, but each system only manages its own buses.

sections.title: The Six Interoperability Rules
sections.content:
Rule 1: All components must agree which component owns each entry's incoming interface, determined by the dispatcher. Rule 2: The component owning an interface decides whether a packet is accepted (with RPF checks and scoped boundaries), but once accepted, all components process it.

Rule 3: When a new (S,G) forwarding entry is created, all components get an alert so they can set their outgoing interfaces. Rule 4: When the last outgoing interface is removed (or none exist at creation), the component owning the incoming interface gets a Prune alert to send upstream. Rule 5: When the first outgoing interface is added, the iif-owning component gets a Join alert.

Rule 6: If a component does not report per-group membership to its interfaces, it must be a wildcard receiver for sources reaching it through other components' interfaces, preventing black holes.
sections.eli5: The rules say: agree on who owns the mailbox, check the address before delivering, tell everyone about new passengers, send cancellations when no one is getting off, send orders when someone wants to board, and stay ready to take everyone's mail if needed.

sections.title: The Alert Dispatcher
sections.content:
The dispatcher is a control component (not tied to any interface) that selects which protocol component owns each entry's incoming interface and decides which components should receive alerts. Two dispatchers are described: the Interop dispatcher for tree topologies of domains without a global inter-domain protocol, and the BGMP dispatcher for use with an inter-domain routing protocol like BGMP.

The Interop dispatcher selects the incoming interface owner by finding the next-hop interface towards the source in the multicast RIB. It handles wildcard entries itself and uses group membership to optimize alert propagation, avoiding broadcast-and-prune between domains when unnecessary.
sections.eli5: The dispatcher is the station manager who decides which bus line owns each route and tells each bus when passengers need to change lines.

sections.title: How Protocols Implement the Rules
sections.content: The RFC gives detailed rules for DVMRP (broadcast-and-prune), MOSPF (link-state, joins whole groups), PIM-DM (dense-mode, like DVMRP), PIM-SM (sparse-mode, uses RPs), CBT (core-based trees), and IGMP-only interfaces. For example, DVMRP sends (S,G) Prune messages when it receives a Prune alert and Graft messages when it receives a Join alert. MOSPF ignores per-source alerts (since it only supports group-level operations) but originates group-membership LSAs when it receives group-level joins. PIM-SM sets the Border-bit in Register messages for externally-reached sources and uses Register-Suppression logic at the RP.
sections.eli5: Each bus system reacts to station orders in its own style: some prune branches, some announce groups, some send join requests. The station just speaks the command language; each system knows how to obey.
